soil-fert-290.title: Trace elements: needed in minute amounts, toxic in excess
soil-fert-290.text: The same element can feed a plant or poison it, and only the dose differs. A trace element is a chemical element present in minute quantity, especially a micronutrient (see {{ref:soil-fert-179}}). Essential ones are needed in tiny amounts for growth and metabolism in plants and animals, and they act as catalysts in {{ref:soil-chem-113}} reactions. Iron, copper, cobalt, iodine, manganese, chlorine, molybdenum, selenium and zinc are essential. Silver, cadmium, mercury and lead are not, and they are toxic to mammals even at low concentration. Some heavy metals in trace amounts act as essential micronutrients, yet every one becomes toxic at high concentrations.

soil-fert-289.title: Mineral nutrients: the elements beyond carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen
soil-fert-289.text:
In nutrition, a mineral is any chemical element other than carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen that an organism needs. A mineral counts only if it is bioavailable, meaning it can be absorbed, so it must be soluble or readily extractable. Metallic molybdenum has no nutritional benefit, while molybdates are sources.

Plants and animals need similar minerals and enzymes, with differences. Legumes host molybdenum-containing nitrogenase, and animals use iron hemoglobin for oxygen but plants do not. Boron is essential to plants but not humans. Silicon is beneficial to most plants but usually not essential. Proving that an element is essential takes a biomolecule containing it with a testable function, because chemically similar elements can be taken up without being essential. Fertilizers are often tailored to the mineral deficiencies of particular soils, such as molybdenum, manganese and zinc.

soil-fert-288.title: Organic matter as the master nutrient strategy
soil-fert-288.text:
If one habit could improve nutrient management overall, the facts name it: raise soil organic matter ({{ref:soil-found-045}}). This is the best overall strategy, especially for nitrogen and phosphorus. Mineralization of phosphorus and sulfur from organic matter is an important source of both, though residues with high C:N ratios can temporarily reduce nitrogen availability.

Organic matter also holds K+, Ca++ and Mg++ ions. It provides natural chelates that keep zinc, copper and manganese in plant-usable forms. Better tilth and growth-promoting substances from decomposition help plants build bigger root systems, and diverse soil organisms keep plant pathogens low. Cover crop roots feed soil organisms that mobilize nutrients and reduce leaching and runoff losses. If legumes, they add nitrogen, and they maintain mycorrhizal spores for the next crop.

soil-fert-286.title: Where nutrient deficiencies tend to appear
soil-fert-286.text:
Of the 17 elements all plants need, only nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are commonly deficient in soils. Sulfur deficiency is less common but not rare. Magnesium, zinc, boron and manganese can be lacking in certain regions. Geography helps predict which (see {{ref:soil-fert-169}}).

Sulfur, magnesium and some micronutrient deficiencies are more common in highly weathered mineral regions, such as the southeastern United States and the tropics, or in high-rainfall regions. Sulfur deficiency is common on sandy coastal-plain soils and in low organic matter soils, as sulfur pollution from coal plants has declined. Calcareous higher-pH soils, especially in dry regions, need watching for iron, zinc, copper and manganese deficiency and for low phosphorus availability. Potassium deficiency is less common in young, little-weathered glaciated soils with moderate to low rainfall, as in the Dakotas.

soil-fert-291.title: Closing the loop on the farm
soil-fert-291.text:
Better on-farm nutrient cycling aims to cut long-distance nutrient flows and return nutrients as residue or manure to the fields they came from. It extends {{ref:soil-fert-192}}.

Losses fall when infiltration and root health rise through organic matter and soil physical management. Apply only the irrigation water needed to refill the root zone, since excess causes runoff and leaching. Rotations with cover crops, perennial grasses and legumes leach less nitrogen than annual row crops such as corn and soybeans. Test manures and credit their nutrients, test soils regularly, and apply most nitrogen near crop uptake.

Add animals to crop farms and match their numbers to the land base. Feeding crops to animals exports far fewer nutrients than selling crops, but animals fed on purchased feed overload a farm. Local organic materials, composting to cut manure weight and volume for transport, compost exchanges and neighboring farm partnerships also help balance flows.

soil-fert-285.title: Manganese: the chlorophyll helper
soil-fert-285.text: Plants short of manganese turn yellow between the leaf veins, a pattern called chlorosis. Manganese activates some enzymes involved in chlorophyll formation, and it is one of the micronutrients in {{ref:soil-fert-179}}. Its availability depends partly on soil pH. The facts add that plants need only trace amounts of nickel, as with other micronutrients. Some plants use molybdenum for nitrogen fixation, so it may need adding to some soils before legumes are sown.

soil-fert-284.title: Copper: electron carrier and cereal limiter
soil-fert-284.text:
Rice and wheat, the two most important food crops, are highly susceptible to copper shortage. Copper is an essential trace element for plants, animals and microorganisms, one of the micronutrients in {{ref:soil-fert-179}}. Its proteins carry electrons and oxygen by easily switching between Cu(I) and Cu(II). All eukaryotes need it for aerobic respiration, and in plants it is a component of some enzymes.

Deficiency shows as browning of leaf tips and chlorosis. Soil copper is not uniform worldwide, and many soils are short of it. Naturally deficient soils often need copper added, usually as copper sulfate, before cereals can be grown, and nitrogen fertilizers can worsen the deficiency. Citrus, oats, spinach and carrots are also highly susceptible, while coconuts, soybeans and asparagus are not very sensitive.

soil-fert-292.title: Fertilizer or organic source: choosing what to apply
soil-fert-292.text:
Commercial fertilizers such as urea, triple superphosphate and muriate of potash are convenient, easy to blend, predictable and precise in timing and rate. They have drawbacks. Common nitrogen materials are acid forming, nitrogen fertilizer takes 25%-50% of the energy in growing corn, and high solubility can cause salt or ammonia damage to seedlings and greater losses if mismanaged. Slow-release forms, such as sulfur- or polymer-coated urea, and nitrification and urease inhibitors, better match supply to crop needs.

Organic sources are the nutrients in crop residues, manures and composts. Organic farmers replace synthetic fertilizers with minerals like greensand, granite dust and rock phosphate, or with bone, fish, soybean and blood meal. The cheapest source is not always best: anhydrous ammonia is hard to inject in stony soil, diammonium phosphate gives 18% N with phosphorus, and potassium magnesium sulfate suits fields needing magnesium but no lime.

soil-fert-287.title: Why nutrient balance protects plants from pests
soil-fert-287.text:
Good nutrient management is critical to general plant health and the control of plant pests ({{ref:soil-fert-192}}). Too much available nitrogen early in the season lets small-seeded weeds with few reserves establish and later out-compete the crop. Nutrient-stressed plants may be stunted, or grow too much foliage and too little fruit when nitrogen is too plentiful, and they emit fewer signals that attract beneficial insects.

Specific imbalances cause specific disorders. Low potassium aggravates stalk rot of corn and winter damage to bermudagrass. Excess potassium in the peanut fruiting zone goes with pod rot, and low calcium with droughty conditions causes tomato blossom-end rot. Healthy plants with large root systems depend on good tilth, no subsurface compaction, drainage, organic matter and a thriving soil biological community.

soil-fert-275.title: Phosphatase: the enzyme that frees phosphate
soil-fert-275.text:
Plants cannot use phosphorus locked in organic molecules until an enzyme cuts it loose. That enzyme is phosphatase, which uses water to cleave a phosphoric acid monoester into a phosphate ion and an alcohol. Phosphatases are hydrolases, working by {{ref:soil-form-172}}: water is split, the -OH joins the phosphate ion and the H+ protonates the alcohol. The monoester is destroyed and free phosphate appears.

Kinases do the opposite job, transferring phosphate from ATP. Phosphorylases are a third group, moving phosphate from hydrogen phosphate to an acceptor. Phosphatases are sorted into 104 enzyme families by substrate specificity and catalytic-domain sequence, yet all run the same general hydrolysis. In soils and ecosystems, phosphatases from roots, microbes and fungi release phosphate from organic phosphorus, which plants can then take up.

soil-fert-276.title: Nutrient flows: sources, destinations and the farm gate
soil-fert-276.text:
Every bag of fertilizer and every truck of grain is a nutrient flow. A flow is the movement of carbon or nutrients from one place to another, linking a source with a destination. Flows happen on a farm, in a grassland or forest, or globally, within the idea of the {{ref:soil-fert-146}}. Buying fertilizer or feed brings nutrients onto the farm, and selling crops, meat or milk sends nutrients and carbon off it.

Flows across the farm gate are managed on purpose. Others are unplanned, such as nitrate leaching to groundwater or runoff carrying nutrients with eroded topsoil. Harvested crops fed to animals and manure returned to the land together make a cycle, because nutrients and carbon come back to the fields they left. Cycling is nearly 100% efficient in forests and natural grassland, but modern specialized farming has little real cycling, with large exports, long bare periods and bigger leaching and runoff losses. Organic matter is over half carbon, so soil nutrient cycling is tied to the carbon cycle.

soil-fert-279.title: Farm nutrient balance: living off capital or building up
soil-fert-279.text:
A farm that exports more than it imports is living off capital. A farm's nutrient balance compares what it imports with what it exports, using the flows in {{ref:soil-fert-276}}. Three patterns result: imports less than, greater than, or equal to exports. A negative balance draws down mineral and organic-matter nutrients until yields fall. Crop farms export a lot per acre each year: about 135 lb N, 25 lb P and 35 lb K for corn grain, and 150 lb N, 20 lb P and 130 lb K for grass hay.

Integrated crop-livestock and grass-fed beef farms keep imports and exports small and near balance, because most nutrients return as manure and urine. Animal farms with too little land for their feed import more than they export. Nutrients build up and may leach or run off, with nitrogen and phosphorus the main water pollutants.

The aim is to bring fertility to optimal levels and then roughly balance inflows and outflows, using soil tests to avoid building up or drawing down too far. Crop farms can balance nutrients in theory, but carbon is hard to replace. Residues do not replace the organic matter lost, which needs manure, compost, intensive cover cropping or perennial hay. Manure must also be spread well across fields, since fields near barns tend to get excess. Soil testing and manure planning can balance each field, and rotational pastures avoid the problem.

soil-fert-278.title: How modern farming broke the nutrient cycle
soil-fert-278.text:
Food travels about 1,300 miles on average from field to consumer. Older farms with crops and animals together cycled carbon and nutrients well, and modern food systems have broken that cycle in successive steps (see {{ref:soil-fert-276}}).

The first break came as cities grew. Nutrients and carbon traveled with farm products to distant urban populations and rarely returned to the soils they came from. City sewage and polluted waterways became sinks for these nutrients, and effluent still carries them into waterways despite new treatment plants. The second break came with farm specialization, which separated animals from the land that grows their feed. Manure accumulates, while crop farmers buy inorganic fertilizer and do not replace lost carbon.

A third, larger-scale break is the shipping of crops across continents and oceans. Nutrients from crop farms travel to animal farms and are replaced by fertilizer from elsewhere, overloading the animal farms. Fertilizer nutrients also travel far, such as potassium from Saskatchewan to Ohio or phosphorus from Morocco to Germany.

soil-fert-283.title: Ion exchange membranes: an artificial root for measuring nitrogen
soil-fert-283.text:
A charged plastic strip can do what a root does. Ion exchange membranes carry charged surface groups that adsorb ions such as NH4+ and NO3- from soil, giving an index of nitrogen supply. They rely on the same charge attraction as {{ref:soil-chem-047}}. They continually remove ammonium and nitrate released from organic N or desorbed from surfaces, mimicking a root, so they measure a supply rate in µg per cm2 per day.

Membranes are buried in the field or used in the lab, then washed and eluted with NaCl (anion) or HCl (cation) before analysis. Plant N uptake related more closely to membrane-adsorbed N than to chemical extractions, so membranes may be a better index of N availability. They are simple, rapid and low cost, with adsorbed N rising with fertilizer rate and varying with season and crop stage.

soil-fert-277.title: Floodplain fertility: rivers that renewed the soil
soil-fert-277.text: Early agriculture centered on low-lying places where rivers converged and flooded fields with sediment. Rivers carry eroded minerals and organic matter downstream and deposit them on low-lying floodplains, renewing the fertility of those soils each year. Monsoon rains in the upper Nile basin brought annual fertile alluvium to the lower valley and delta, sustaining a large population for several millennia. Other ancient centers on alluvial deposits include the Indo-Gangetic Plain, the North China Plain, Mesopotamia and the Valley of Mexico.

soil-fert-280.title: The nitrogen balance: a simple test of sustainable use
soil-fert-280.text:
One subtraction can tell whether a field's nitrogen use is sustainable. The N balance is N inputs from nutrient additions minus N outputs in the harvested crop over a season, a check on the {{ref:soil-fert-099}}. The optimum is generally between 0 and +50 pounds per acre. Below 0 the soil is being mined of nitrogen, and above 50 the excess causes environmental damage. The 50 pounds allowance reflects that N use is never fully efficient and some leaching and N2O losses are unavoidable.

Most grain farms in the developed world import more N than they export, so their balance is positive. Reaching the optimum range takes careful N management with 4R practices and end-of-season cover crops, and rotations with low-leaching crops lower average losses.

soil-fert-281.title: Losing nitrogen even when the books balance
soil-fert-281.text:
A farm can import and export nearly equal nitrogen and still pollute. In high-yielding corn, roughly 150-160 lb N applied matches the 160 lb in the grain, but much of the applied N is tied up in organic matter or lost by leaching or denitrification. Corn needs large amounts of nitrate daily during its two-month growth spurt. Pollution arises when fertilizer, manure and decomposing organic matter together supply far more than the crop needs.

Leftover nitrate after harvest can leach into groundwater in fall, winter or early spring, at roughly 30-70 pounds per acre depending on precipitation, and some may become nitrous oxide. Losses are reduced by predicting crop needs from all N sources, timing application close to crop demand, and planting a quick-establishing cover crop.

soil-fert-282.title: Grain trade as a nutrient pipeline
soil-fert-282.text:
Every shipload of grain carries soil with it, in the form of nutrients and carbon. Traded grain and oilseed crops move these between regions, leaving deficiencies in exporting soils and excesses in importing ones. The biggest transfers are corn and soybeans shipped from the Americas to East Asia, Europe and the Middle East, driven by demand for animal protein and oils. The United States, Brazil and Argentina supply almost 90% of soybean and 75% of corn exports, and South America has met demand by converting grassland, savannah and rainforest to crops.

Exporting regions show less healthy breadbasket soils that have lost organic matter. Importing countries accumulate nutrients on livestock farms and see hypoxia in nearby seas. Trade can also help: importing U.S. wheat raises selenium intake in Europe.
